answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — a 20th-century addition
answer.authorName: Unknown — first known in print in 1989
answer.authorDates: Earliest known appearance in print: Orlando Sentinel, 22 June 1989
answer.sourceLine: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello classifies this as a spurious quotation: it “has not been found in any of the writings of Thomas Jefferson.” Monticello dates its earliest known appearance in print to 1989, footnoting a pro–Second Amendment column by Charley Reese in the Orlando Sentinel. It is usually bolted onto a sentence Jefferson really did draft — “No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms” — which is why the whole thing reads as authentic.
answer.confidenceText: No Jefferson manuscript, letter, or published text contains this sentence; the earliest documented appearance is a 1989 newspaper column.

trail: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation lists the sentence among its spurious quotations, stating it “has not been found in any of the writings of Thomas Jefferson” and giving 1989 as the earliest known appearance in print — Monticello ↗.
Monticello’s own quotation database files it as a Spurious Quote — Jefferson Quotes & Family Letters ↗.
The genuine clause is documented with its citation in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, 1:344, 353, 363 — Extract from Jefferson’s Drafts of the Virginia Constitution ↗.
PolitiFact ↗ rated the circulating version False, reporting that Monticello places both sentences of the meme on its spurious list.
source.excerptNote: That is the authentic sentence, from Jefferson’s second draft of a constitution for Virginia. The famous continuation — “The strongest reason for the people to retain the right to keep and bear arms is, as a last resort, to protect themselves against tyranny in government” — appears in no Jefferson draft, letter, or publication.

source.rightsNote: Jefferson’s genuine 1776 draft clause is long in the public domain. The disputed sentence is a different matter: no author or first publication has been established for it, and its earliest documented appearance is a 1989 newspaper column, which would itself be in copyright. Because the wording’s origin is unresolved, we assert no rights status for it.

author.name: Thomas Jefferson
author.heading: About Thomas Jefferson
author.metaLine: 1743–1826 · Author of the Declaration of Independence; third U.S. president
author.bio: Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, served as third president of the United States, and left one of the most completely documented paper trails of any founder — tens of thousands of letters and papers, now searchable through The Papers of Thomas Jefferson and Founders Online. That completeness is exactly why spurious quotations are catchable: if a sentence is nowhere in the corpus, its absence is meaningful. Jefferson did write about arms — his 1776 draft constitution for Virginia proposed that “No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms” — but that clause never entered the constitution as adopted, and it carries none of the language about tyranny that circulates today.

cite.sourceCitation: “Strongest reason for the people to retain the right to keep and bear arms… (Spurious Quotation),” Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia, Thomas Jefferson Foundation, Monticello. Monticello records the earliest known appearance in print as 1989, citing Charley Reese, “Founding Fathers Gave Individuals the Right to Bear Arms,” Orlando Sentinel, 22 June 1989. The genuine adjacent clause, “No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms,” appears in Jefferson’s drafts of a constitution for Virginia, before 13 June 1776, in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, 1:344, 353, 363.

copyAttribution: Not Thomas Jefferson. "The strongest reason for the people to retain the right to keep and bear arms is, as a last resort, to protect themselves against tyranny in government" is listed by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello as a spurious quotation, not found in any of Jefferson's writings; its earliest known appearance in print is a 1989 Orlando Sentinel column. Only the sentence it is usually paired with — "No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms," from Jefferson's 1776 Virginia constitution drafts — is genuine. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: How the fake got its authority
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared quotations in American gun-rights debate, and it fails on the simplest test: it is nowhere in Jefferson.

items.why: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation files it under spurious quotations, stating that it “has not been found in any of the writings of Thomas Jefferson” after searches of the Papers of Thomas Jefferson Digital Edition, the Retirement Series, and HathiTrust — see Monticello ↗.

“No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms” is authentic Jefferson, from his drafts of a constitution for Virginia (before 13 June 1776), printed in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, 1:344 — and the language was never adopted into the constitution Virginia enacted. See Monticello ↗. Attaching the tyranny sentence to it is what makes the forgery convincing.

items.scope: The companion line in the same meme
items.why: The version that circulates on social media usually opens “When governments fear the people, there is liberty…” — which PolitiFact ↗ reports Monticello traced to a 1914 published debate on socialism, in which John Basil Barnhill wrote: “Where the people fear the government you have tyranny. Where the government fears the people you have liberty.”

Monticello’s entry gives the earliest known appearance in print as 1989, footnoting Charley Reese, “Founding Fathers Gave Individuals the Right to Bear Arms,” Orlando Sentinel, 22 June 1989, and notes the sentence then “appeared in a number of publications in quick succession in the mid-1990s” — Monticello ↗. That is the earliest sighting on record, not proof of who coined it.

misattribution.truthLine: Jefferson proposed that no freeman be debarred the use of arms. The sentence about tyranny is a modern addition to his words, first recorded in print in 1989 — per the Thomas Jefferson Foundation ↗.

context.heading: Why this one spread so well
lead: The sentence is engineered to pass. It is grafted onto a line Jefferson really wrote — “No freeman shall be debarred the use of arms,” from his 1776 draft constitution for Virginia — so a reader who checks the first half finds a real citation and stops checking. Monticello notes the pairing explicitly: the spurious sentence “is often seen preceded by” the genuine clause.

It also sounds like Jefferson without reading like him. “Retain the right to keep and bear arms” borrows Second Amendment phrasing that postdates the Virginia drafts, and “as a last resort” is the cadence of modern op-ed writing, not eighteenth-century constitutional drafting. Monticello’s researchers searched the Papers of Thomas Jefferson Digital Edition, the Retirement Series, and HathiTrust and came up empty.
detailsBody: Jefferson wrote three drafts of a constitution for Virginia in mid-1776. The first draft reads “No freeman shall ever be debarred the use of arms”; the second and third add the limitation “within his own lands or tenements.” The texts are printed in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, 1:344, 353, 363, and are online at Founders Online ↗.
None of this language was adopted into the Virginia Constitution of 1776, and none of the drafts contains anything about tyranny in government.
context.pull: Half of it is real. That is the whole trick.
